narratives.narrative: Aheb here (sense 7691307) is read as affect (type 7691308) but a DISORDERED one: the operation (7691311) is that the sons of men turn their own honour into shame precisely because they love empty things and chase after lies - misdirected desire. The bearer (7691310) is 'the men', the opponents; the target (7691312) is not a good object but 'misdirected-love' itself, and the coupling (7691314) welds love to vanity (love-vanity). Locus is internal:ib-state (7691315) with role characteristic (7691317): this is genuinely an inner-being movement, the interior fastening on emptiness (discovery 7691316). The silences carry weight. There is NO source (103 absent): the psalm does not trace where this love comes from, only that it grips. There is NO seat (7691309='none'): the disordered love is not organ-located, it is diffused through the whole self, not lodged in heart or kidneys. Manner is 'none' (7691313) - no qualifying mode is given; the love is bare, unmodulated appetite. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): the passage does not measure how hot this love burns, adds no further specification, records no downstream effect, and issues no explicit ban - the diagnosis stands as bare description of a self bent toward the vain. Read without valence-comfort, this is love operating as ruin: the same faculty that elsewhere clings to God here binds a person to lies and hollows out his own honour.
narratives.story: Here the psalmist turns on his opponents and names what is wrong inside them: they love empty, worthless things and run after lies, and in doing so they trade their own honour for shame. It is real love - a genuine pull of the heart - but pointed at nothing, at vanity. The psalm does not say where this craving came from or where in them it sits; it simply grips the whole person. It measures no heat and pronounces no verdict beyond the plain fact: a self can fasten itself to emptiness, and when it does, it quietly destroys its own dignity.
narratives.variation_note: Of the 13 readings of aheb in this family, this is the clearest DESCENT: love as misdirected appetite (bearer = the opponents, target = vanity/lies, locus internal), where nearly every other reading has love pointed at God, his name, house, law or salvation. The difference is the whole finding - the same verb runs downward here.

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7691584) is affect (type 7691585): those who love God's NAME. The bearer (7691587) is 'those who love the name'; the operation (7691588) is love of the name overflowing into exultation, and the target (7691589) is 'name-love' - love aimed specifically at who God is as revealed in his name. The coupling (7691591, love-and-exult) welds the love to jubilation: this love does not stay quiet but breaks into song. Locus is internal:ib-state (7691592), role characteristic (7691594): the exultation springs from an inner attachment, not merely from being sheltered (discovery 7691593 marks this as distinct from refuge-joy). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the psalm does not derive the love, it simply attaches; NO seat (7691586='none') - not organ-located, the whole self loves; manner 'none' (7691590) - the love is unqualified, direct. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition all absent (109-113): the passage does not gauge the fervour, adds nothing further, names no separate consequence beyond the exultation already given in the coupling, and forbids nothing. The reading holds a real distinction: joy here is not the relief of the protected but the overflow of love for God's very identity.
narratives.story: The psalm ends by picturing those who love God's name breaking out in glad singing. Their joy is not just relief at being kept safe - it rises specifically from loving who God is. Love and rejoicing are bound together here: to love him this way is to overflow into song. The psalm does not explain how the love began or locate it in any one part of the person; the whole self simply loves and exults. Nothing more is measured or added - the picture is a people so taken with God's name that gladness pours out of them.
narratives.variation_note: Unlike #1 (disordered love of vanity) and the later law-love readings, this aheb targets God's NAME and its distinctive fruit is exultation (coupling love-and-exult); the finding is that love of God's identity, not mere shelter, is what breaks into joy.

narratives.narrative: This is racham (sense 7693986), the rare and tender verb of womb-love, read as affect (type 7693987): 'I love you, O LORD, my strength.' The bearer (7693989) is the psalmist himself; the operation (7693990) is the self DECLARING a tender, intimate love for the LORD its strength - and strikingly this whole deliverance-song opens not with thanks but with affection (discovery 7693995). The target (7693991) is 'tender-love', and the coupling (7693993, love-you-LORD) binds the love directly to the LORD as its object. Locus internal:ib-state (7693994), role characteristic (7693996). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the love is not derived from the deliverance that follows; it stands first, as if the rescue flows from the bond rather than the bond from the rescue; NO seat (7693988='none') - the intimate love is not lodged in a single organ but is the posture of the whole self; manner 'none' (7693992) - no qualifying mode, the love is bare and direct. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113): the passage does not measure the warmth, add specification, name a separate effect, or prohibit. The finding is that the interior movement opening the great rescue psalm is warm attachment - love as the first word, softer and more intimate than gratitude.
narratives.story: The great song of rescue opens not with 'thank you' but with 'I love you.' The word used is unusually tender - the kind of love a mother has in her body for her child - and it is aimed straight at the LORD, whom the psalmist calls his strength. This affection comes first, before any account of being saved, as though the love is the root and the rescue the fruit. The psalm does not say where the love began or place it in any one part of him; his whole self simply leans toward God in warmth. It is the quietest and most intimate opening he could have chosen.

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7696187) is affect (type 7696188): 'O LORD, I love the habitation of your house and the place where your glory dwells.' The bearer (7696190) is the psalmist singular; the operation (7696191) is the self loving God's dwelling-place, the very site where his glory resides (discovery 7696196). The target (7696192) is 'love-of-the-house', and the coupling (7696194, love-your-house) fastens the affection to the sanctuary. Locus internal:ib-state (7696195), role characteristic (7696197). The distinction preserved here: the love is aimed not at God directly, nor at his name (5:11) or law, but at his HOUSE - the place of presence. The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the psalm, set amid protests of integrity, does not derive the love; NO seat (7696189='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7696193) - unqualified. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition all absent (109-113): no measure of fervour, no further specification, no named downstream effect, no prohibition. Set within a psalm defending the psalmist's separation from evildoers, this love of the sanctuary functions as the positive counterpart to his hatred of the assembly of the wicked - the interior drawn toward the place where glory dwells.
narratives.story: In a psalm where the writer insists he has kept clear of liars and wrongdoers, he names what he is drawn TO: 'I love the house where you live, the place where your glory dwells.' His love here reaches not for God in the abstract but for the very place of God's presence. It is the warm opposite of his refusal to sit with the wicked. The psalm does not say how this love arose or fix it in any single part of him; the whole self simply longs for that place. It is affection for where God can be found.
narratives.variation_note: Among the aheb readings, this one's target is God's HOUSE/dwelling-place (not his name, law, salvation, or God himself), and it works as the positive mirror of the psalm's hatred of the wicked's assembly.

narratives.narrative: Uniquely among these aheb readings, the type is VOLITION (7697217), not affect: 'Love the LORD, all you his saints!' The sense (7697216) is love the LORD, but here it arrives as an imperative summons. The bearer (7697219) is 'the saints', the community being called; the operation (7697220) is the self turning its personal deliverance into a call - drawing the whole community into love and confidence, since the LORD preserves the faithful but repays the proud (discovery 7697225). The target (7697221) is 'summoning-love', and the coupling (7697223, love-the-LORD) binds the summons to its object. Locus internal:ib-state (7697224), role characteristic (7697226). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - though contextually the summons flows from the rescue just recounted, the love itself is not derived; NO seat (7697218='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7697222) - the command is unqualified. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113): no measured fervour, no further specification, no separate named effect, no prohibition. The finding is that love here is not reported as a feeling but WILLED and commanded outward - the interior, having been delivered, moves to enlist others' interiors in the same love.
narratives.story: After being rescued, the psalmist does not simply feel grateful - he turns to everyone around him and commands, 'Love the LORD, all you his faithful ones!' His love here is not a private feeling being described but a summons being issued: he wants the whole community to love God as he does, because God guards the faithful and pays back the proud. The psalm does not say where this love comes from or locate it in any part of the person; it is a deliberate act of the will, reaching outward. Having been saved himself, he moves to draw others into the same devotion.
narratives.variation_note: This is the ONLY aheb reading typed as volition (a commanded summons) rather than affect/disposition; the bearer is the whole community being enlisted, not an individual reporting a feeling - love here is willed and broadcast outward.

narratives.narrative: Here the love-word surfaces as its social relation - 'my friends' (sense 7699615, the loving ones / those bound in affection) - and the type is STATE (7699616), not an act of loving but a condition undergone. The bearer (7699618) is the psalmist; the operation (7699619) is that his friends and companions stand aloof from his plague while his nearest kin stand far off - the isolation of the afflicted (discovery 7699624). The target (7699620) is 'abandonment', and the coupling (7699622, friends-aloof) fixes the relation as withdrawal. Locus internal:ib-state (7699623), role characteristic (7699625): the wound registered is inward, the felt emptiness of desertion. The silences are eloquent. NO source (103 absent) - the psalm does not explain WHY the friends withdraw, only that they do; NO seat (7699617='none') - the pain is not organ-located but pervades the whole self; manner 'none' (7699621) - the desertion is bare, unqualified. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113): the passage does not measure the grief of it, adds nothing further, names no separate consequence, forbids nothing. Read without filtering the uncomfortable: love appears here in its failure - the room emptied of everyone, affection's covenant broken from the other side, the sufferer left with the ache of those who should have loved and did not.
narratives.story: Crushed by sickness and guilt, the psalmist looks around and finds himself alone: his friends and companions keep their distance from his suffering, and even his closest relatives stand far off. Love appears here by its absence - the people who should have stayed have pulled away. The psalm does not explain why they left or where exactly the hurt lands; it simply names the empty room. It does not even measure the grief. This is affection in collapse, the wound of being deserted by those nearest, and it is felt deep inside.

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7650303) as action (type 7650304): the king 'has loved righteousness and hated wickedness.' The bearer (7650306) is the king; the operation (7650307) is love, and the target (7650308) is righteousness, recorded as a span-resolved PAIR (from 278985 to 278986) - the love is grounded in the actual words of the verse. Crucially the coupling (7650310) is also a span-pair (to 278987): this love is welded to its opposite, the hatred of wickedness - the two moral affections operate as a single hinge, and together they are the ground of the king's anointing 'with the oil of gladness' (discovery 7650312). Locus internal:ib-state (7650311), role characteristic (7650313). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the love of right is not traced to a cause, it simply defines him; NO seat (7650305='none') - not organ-located, it is the set of the whole royal self; manner 'none' (7650309) - the love is unqualified. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113): no measured degree, no further specification, no separate named effect, no prohibition. The finding: love here is a moral orientation, not warmth toward a person - to love righteousness AND hate wickedness together is the interior that qualifies one to reign.
narratives.story: The royal psalm praises the king for the shape of his heart: he has loved what is right and hated what is wrong. These two go together as one movement - to love righteousness is at the same time to hate wickedness - and this is exactly why God has honoured and anointed him above his peers. His love is not warmth toward a person but a settled bent of character toward the good. The psalm does not explain how it arose or place it in any one part of him; it is simply who he is, and it is what makes him fit to rule.
narratives.variation_note: Among the three 'loved' (aheb participle) readings, this alone is a POSITIVE moral affection (love of righteousness, welded to hatred of wickedness) borne by the king; #2 is the enemy's love of cursing and #3 is love of God's promise.

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7652797) as action (type 7652798), read at full descent: 'You love evil more than good.' The bearer (7652800) is the tyrant; the operation (7652801) is love/prefer, and the target (7652802) is evil, recorded as a span-pair (from 279812 to 279813) - the love genuinely fastens on evil. The manner (7652803) is itself a pair (to 279815): 'more than good' - this love is comparative, a weighing that chooses evil over its rival. The coupling (7652804, span-pair to 279816) binds it to a parallel inversion: loving lying over truthful speech. Locus internal:ib-state (7652805), role characteristic (7652807): this is a real inner-being movement, the disordered heart whose loves are turned upside down (discovery 7652806). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the psalm does not explain how the loves became inverted; NO seat (7652799='none') - not organ-located, the inversion pervades the whole self; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, no further specification, no separately named consequence, and notably NO prohibition, even here where evil is loved: the text describes rather than forbids. Read without valence-comfort, this is the love-faculty working in reverse - the very capacity that elsewhere clings to God here prefers evil to good and lies to truth.
narratives.story: The psalm exposes a powerful, boastful man by naming what he loves: he loves evil more than good, and lying more than honest speech. This is love genuinely at work, but flipped upside down - a heart that weighs good against evil and deliberately chooses the worse. The psalm does not say how his loves got twisted or fix the fault in any one part of him; the whole man is bent this way. It does not even stop to forbid it - it simply shows it. The same power to love that can cling to God is here running in reverse.
narratives.variation_note: A DESCENT reading paired with #6 (same tyrant, next verse): here the inverted love's target is evil-over-good and lying-over-truth (a comparative preference); #6 keeps the same inversion but shifts the target to devouring speech.

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7652830) as action (type 7652831), the same inverted love as v3 now fixed on speech: 'You love all words that devour, O deceitful tongue.' The bearer (7652833) is the tyrant; the operation (7652834) is love, the target (7652835) is 'all words that devour', and the manner (7652836) qualifies it as 'words that devour' - destroying speech. The coupling (7652837) is a span-pair back to v3 (from 279821 to 279812): the text itself links this love to the inverted love of the previous verse, marking them as one continuous disorder. Locus internal:ib-state (7652838), role characteristic (7652840): the relish for ruinous speech is an inner-being movement - he does not merely speak evil, he DELIGHTS in the ruin his words work (discovery 7652839). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the relish is not derived; NO seat (7652832='none') - not organ-located; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - the wreck the words cause is not separately tallied as an effect, no degree is measured, nothing further specified, and again no prohibition is issued. The finding, held distinct from v3: the inverted love has narrowed from a general preference for evil to a specific appetite - a love of the devouring word, affection bonded to destruction through the tongue.
narratives.story: A verse later the same twisted love is described again, but now aimed precisely at cruel words: this man loves speech that devours, that tears people down. He does not merely speak evil - he takes pleasure in the damage his words do. The psalm itself ties this back to the previous verse, treating it as one unbroken disorder. It does not explain where the appetite came from, locate it in any single part of him, or tally up the wreckage it causes; it simply names the delight. His love has narrowed to a taste for destruction carried on the tongue.
narratives.variation_note: Paired with #5: the coupling (7652837) explicitly ties this back to v3's inverted love, but the target narrows from a broad preference for evil to a specific appetite for devouring speech - the disorder localises in the tongue.

narratives.narrative: This is yadid (sense 7655740), the passive relation of being dearly loved, and the type is STATUS (7655741), not an act of loving but the condition of being God's beloved - 'that your beloved ones may be delivered.' Uniquely in this family a SOURCE is present (7655748, span-pair to 280825): the beloved are those whom God saves by his right hand and answers - their belovedness is defined by God's saving action toward them. The bearer (7655743) is the beloved people (yedidim); the operation (7655744, span-pair to 280824) is 'be delivered' - the beloved are acted upon, not acting. The target (7655745) is 'none' - fittingly, since being loved has no object it reaches toward; the movement runs FROM God TO them. Manner (7655746) is 'by God's right hand'. The coupling (7655747, span-pair to 280818) identifies the beloved with 'those who fear God' of v4. Locus external:god (7655749), role characteristic (7655751): the state is constituted by God, its ground lies outside the self in his love (discovery 7655750 - they appeal not to merit but to being loved). The silences: NO seat (7655742='none'); intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, no separate effect, no prohibition. The finding: love here is received, not given - the people plead on the ground of being loved, and their whole standing rests outside themselves in God.
narratives.story: The people, under God's discipline, make their plea on one ground: they are his beloved. Notice the direction - they are not loving here, they are LOVED; their standing comes entirely from God's affection for them and his willingness to rescue them by his own strong hand. Their prayer does not point to anything they have earned; it points to who they are to him. The psalm ties these beloved ones to those who fear God, and rests their whole hope outside themselves - in the fact that God loves them and will save them. Being loved, not loving, is the anchor of the prayer.

narratives.narrative: Dabaq (sense 7656534), the verb of cleaving used for a man cleaving to his wife, as action (type 7656535): 'My soul clings to you.' Alone among the readings of this family, a SEAT is named (7656536, span-pair 302642->302641): the SOUL - the clinging is lodged in the nephesh, not diffused. The bearer (7656537, same span-pair) is the psalmist by way of his soul; the operation (7656538) is cling/cleave; the target (7656539) is God. The manner (7656540) is 'held fast by God's upholding right hand', and the coupling (7656541, span-pair to 302646) records the mutual grip: as the soul clings, God's right hand upholds him - the grasp is secured from both sides (discovery 7656543). Locus external:god (7656542), role characteristic (7656544): the movement terminates outside the self, in God. The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the clinging is not derived from a prior cause; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, no separately named effect, no prohibition. The finding, sharpened by the presence of a seat: this is love as total attachment concentrated in the soul, and it is answered - the soul's cleaving to God is met by God's hand holding on in return, a double hold.
narratives.story: Out in the wilderness, thirsty for God, the psalmist says his very soul clings to him - the same word used for a husband holding fast to his wife. This is love as total attachment, and here it is felt right at the core of him, in his soul. And it is not one-sided: as he clings, God's strong hand is holding him up in return. The grip runs both ways, secured from both sides. The psalm does not explain how the clinging began or measure its strength; it simply shows a soul fastened to God and a God who will not let go.
narratives.variation_note: The ONLY reading in the family with a named seat (the soul), and the only cling directed at GOD with a mutual grip (God's hand upholds in return); #2 clings downward to the dust and #3 to God's testimonies.

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7660243) as action (type 7660244): 'those who love his name shall dwell in it.' A SOURCE is present here (7660251, span-pair to 306609): the love and its inheritance arise because God will save Zion (v35) - the settled love of the redeemed community grows out of God's saving act. The bearer (7660246) is 'the offspring of God's servants'; the operation (7660247) is love; the target (7660248, span-pair to 281857) is God's NAME. The manner (7660249) is 'dwelling in the restored Zion' - the love is lived out as settled habitation. Notably the coupling (7660250) is 'none': unlike other name-love readings this love is not welded to a further movement; it stands complete in dwelling. Locus external:god (7660252), role characteristic (7660254): a psalm that began as the lament of a drowning man closes on the settled love of God's name that marks his true people (discovery 7660253). The silences: NO seat (7660245='none') - not organ-located; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, no separate effect, no prohibition. The finding: love here is generational and inheriting - born of salvation, directed at God's name, and expressed simply by belonging to the place God has saved.
narratives.story: The psalm has moved from a man crying out as if drowning to a final, settled picture: the children of God's servants, those who love his name, will live in the rescued city of Zion. Their love grows straight out of God's saving work - because he will save Zion, a people who love his name will inherit it. This love is not restless or reaching for anything more; it simply dwells there, at home. The psalm does not root it in any one part of them or measure it; it marks who they are - a lasting, inheriting people whose love for God's name is expressed by belonging to the place he has saved.
narratives.variation_note: One of two aheb readings with a SOURCE present (love arises 'because God will save Zion'); unlike #2's name-love that overflows in exultation, this one's coupling is 'none' - it rests complete in dwelling, a generational/inheriting love.

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7660724) as action (type 7660725): 'those who love your salvation.' The bearer (7660727) is 'those who love God's salvation'; the operation (7660728) is love; the target (7660729, span-pair to 282023) is God's SALVATION - not God himself, nor his name, but his saving WORK. The manner (7660730, span-pair to 282027) is 'saying evermore, God is great', and the coupling (7660731, same span) records that this love issues in magnifying God evermore: the love overflows into continual praise. Locus external:god (7660732), role characteristic (7660734): loving what God does for the lost is the inner attachment that drives the endless acclaim (discovery 7660733). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the love is not traced to a cause; NO seat (7660726='none') - not organ-located; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, and the ongoing praise is captured in manner/coupling rather than as a separate effect; no prohibition. The finding, held distinct from the name-love and God-love readings: the object here is God's saving action - to love his salvation is to love what he does to rescue, and that love cannot stay silent, it keeps declaring his greatness.
narratives.story: In this urgent cry for help, the psalmist pictures the kind of people he longs to see vindicated: those who love God's saving help. Their love is aimed at what God DOES to rescue - his salvation - and it cannot keep quiet. It keeps overflowing into praise: they say, again and again, 'God is great!' The psalm does not explain how their love began or place it in any one part of them; it simply shows that loving God's rescue makes a person unable to stop celebrating it. Their affection for his saving work turns into endless, glad acclaim.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct target among aheb readings: God's SALVATION (his saving work), not his name/law/house/self; its coupling shows the love overflowing specifically into continual praise ('God is great').

narratives.narrative: Chashaq (sense 7669388), a verb of clinging attachment, as disposition (type 7669389): 'Because he holds fast to me in love, I will deliver him.' Notably these are GOD's own words about the one who loves him, yet the characteristic read is the human interior. The bearer (7669391) is 'the one who loves God'; the operation (7669392) is to hold fast in love; the target (7669393) is God. The coupling field (7669395) carries 'external:god' - the attachment is bound to God as its object; and the locus field (7669396) records that the love is paired with 'knowing God's name' (v14b: 'because he knows my name'): love and knowledge of God run together. Role characteristic (7669398). This clinging love is the GROUND of God's deliverance (discovery 7669397) - God moves to rescue BECAUSE the person holds fast to him. The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the love is not derived; NO seat (7669390='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7669394) - unqualified; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, and the deliverance, though promised, is framed as God's response rather than logged here as the characteristic's own effect; no prohibition. The finding: from God's side, a person's clinging love is what he answers - the human interior fastening on him is met, cause to consequence, by rescue, protection, answer, and honour.
narratives.story: God himself speaks here about the person who loves him: 'Because he holds fast to me in love, I will rescue him.' The love described is a clinging, a refusal to let go, and it runs hand in hand with truly knowing God. And this love is the reason for everything God promises next - deliverance, protection, answered prayer, honour. The person holds on, and God responds. The psalm does not explain where the love came from or place it in any one part of the person; it simply shows a life fastened to God, and a God who answers that grip with rescue.

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7671099) as disposition (type 7671100): 'O you who love the LORD, hate evil!' The bearer (7671102) is 'those who love God'; the operation (7671103) is love; the target (7671104) is the LORD himself - direct, not his name or work. The coupling field (7671106) carries 'external:god'; the locus field (7671107) records that the love is paired with 'hating evil' - the two set as one disposition. The love of God is read as the GROUND of the moral charge: because you love the LORD, hate evil - devotion that shapes conduct (discovery 7671108). Role characteristic (7671109). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the love is assumed, not derived; NO seat (7671101='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7671105) - unqualified; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, no separately logged effect (the moral demand is carried in the locus-pairing rather than as effect), and though evil is to be hated, no prohibition is recorded on the love itself. The finding: love of God is not an isolated warmth but a disposition with a necessary shape - to love the LORD is to be turned against evil; the interior attachment carries an ethical demand within it.
narratives.story: The psalm addresses those who love the LORD and immediately draws a line from that love to a way of living: 'you who love the LORD, hate evil.' The love is aimed straight at God himself, and it is not meant to sit alone as a warm feeling - loving him means turning against what is evil. The one implies the other. The psalm does not explain how the love arose or locate it in any single part of the person; it treats the love as already there and shows what it demands. To love God is, of itself, to hate evil.
narratives.variation_note: Among the aheb readings this one targets the LORD directly (not his name/law/salvation) and its distinctive feature is the ethical pairing (locus: paired with hating evil) - love of God as a disposition that shapes conduct.

narratives.narrative: Ahabah (sense 7677103), the noun 'love', as disposition (type 7677104): 'In return for my love they accuse me.' The bearer (7677106) is the psalmist; the operation (7677107) is love; the target (7677108) is 'his accusers' - the love was directed toward the very people who now turn on him. The coupling field (7677110) carries 'internal:ib-state', and the locus field (7677111) records the love as paired with 'the accusation returned for it': the love is defined here by what it MEETS - hostility. Role characteristic (7677113). The psalmist's goodwill is met with accusation, love repaid with enmity (discovery 7677112); his own response is to give himself to prayer. The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the love is not derived; NO seat (7677105='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7677109) - unqualified; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, no separately logged effect, no prohibition. The finding: love here is real and outward-directed but UNREQUITED and worse - it is answered with attack. The characteristic is shown in its vulnerability: to love others is to expose oneself, and the exposure can be exploited.
narratives.story: The psalmist describes a bitter reversal: he loved these people, and in return they accuse him. His love was genuine and aimed right at them, but it was thrown back as hostility. The psalm does not explain how his love began or place it in any one part of him; it defines the love by what it ran into - not warmth returned, but attack. His only recourse is to turn to prayer. Here love is shown at its most exposed: to love someone is to make yourself vulnerable to them, and that openness can be used against you.
narratives.variation_note: Paired with #2 (same psalm, next verse): #1's love is met with ACCUSATION (target = the accusers, locus = accusation returned); #2 escalates - the same love met with HATRED.

narratives.narrative: Ahabah (sense 7677169), 'love', as disposition (type 7677170): 'and hatred for my love.' The bearer (7677172) is the psalmist; the operation (7677173) is love; the target (7677174) is 'his enemies'. The coupling field (7677176) carries 'internal:ib-state', and the locus field (7677177) records the love as paired with 'the hatred returned': the exchange is love-for-hatred, evil-for-good. Role characteristic (7677179). The psalmist's love is answered with hatred (discovery 7677178) - the same disposition as v4, but the return has escalated from accusation to open hatred. The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the love is not derived; NO seat (7677171='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7677175) - unqualified; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, no separately logged effect, no prohibition. The finding, held distinct from v4: the two verses trace a deepening - first accusation, now hatred - so that the same outward love meets a hardening return. Read without flinching, this is the interior of goodwill colliding with settled enmity; the psalm's ensuing torrent of curses is the answer of a love that has been repaid with hate.
narratives.story: A verse later the psalmist names the exchange even more starkly: 'they give me hatred in return for my love.' It is the same real love as before, aimed at these people, but now what comes back is not merely accusation but outright hatred. The two verses together show it deepening - first they accused him, now they hate him. The psalm does not explain the love's origin or locate it anywhere in him; it simply measures it against the hostility it draws. This is goodwill running straight into settled hatred, and it sets the stage for the psalm's furious response.
narratives.variation_note: Paired with #1: same love, but the return escalates from accusation (v4) to HATRED (v5), and the target is named 'his enemies' rather than 'his accusers' - the two readings trace a hardening exchange.

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7677345) as disposition (type 7677346), at full descent: 'He loved to curse; let curses come upon him!' The bearer (7677348) is the enemy; the operation (7677349) is love; the target (7677350) is 'to curse' - the love is fastened on the ACT of cursing. The coupling field (7677352) carries 'internal:ib-state', and the locus field (7677353) records the love as paired with 'cursing and the absence of delight in blessing': the same verse notes 'he did not delight in blessing', so the disordered love is doubled by a matching aversion - he loves to curse and takes no pleasure in blessing. Role characteristic (7677355). This is the enemy's delight in cursing, now recoiling on him (discovery 7677354) - the curse he loved returns as his portion. The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the love is not derived; NO seat (7677347='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7677351) - unqualified; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, and though the psalm prays the curse back on him, that recoil is framed as petition rather than logged as the characteristic's own effect; no prohibition. The finding: love here is bonded to harm - a person can love cursing itself, and the absence of any love of blessing completes the portrait of an interior set toward ruin.
narratives.story: The psalm turns to describe the enemy's inner bent: he loved to curse, and he took no pleasure in blessing. His love was fixed on the act of cursing itself, matched by a coldness toward blessing - the two together showing a heart set toward harm. So the psalm prays that the very cursing he loved would come back on him as his own portion. It does not explain how his love got so twisted or locate it in any one part of him; it simply shows a person who loved to wound and had no taste for good. His love and his lack of love point the same direction: toward ruin.
narratives.variation_note: The DESCENT reading among the three 'loved' (aheb participle) items: borne by the enemy, its target is the act of cursing (doubled by the absence of delight in blessing), where #1 loves righteousness and #3 loves God's promise.

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7679165) as disposition (type 7679166): 'I love the LORD, because he has heard my voice and my pleas for mercy.' The bearer (7679168) is the psalmist; the operation (7679169) is love; the target (7679170) is the LORD himself. The coupling field (7679172) carries 'external:god', and the locus field (7679173) records the love as paired with 'God hearing his pleas': the affection is expressly born of answered prayer (discovery 7679174). Role characteristic (7679175). Though no formal source-row is recorded (103 absent), the locus-pairing supplies the ground in the text itself - the love answers God's hearing; this is devotion as response, love kindled by having been heard. The silences: NO seat (7679167='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7679171) - unqualified; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, no separately logged effect, no prohibition. The finding: love here is reactive in the best sense - not commanded, not moral orientation, but the warm turning of the self toward a God who listened. The interior loves BECAUSE it was heard; the answered cry is the spring of the affection.
narratives.story: The psalm opens simply: 'I love the LORD, because he has heard my voice and my cry for mercy.' This love is a response - it rises precisely because God listened when the psalmist was desperate. He does not command it or reason his way into it; it is the warm turning of a rescued person toward the God who answered. The psalm does not locate the love in any one part of him or measure it; it just names its cause: he was heard. Being listened to in his need is what kindled his love.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct among aheb readings: love of the LORD directly, expressly kindled as RESPONSE to answered prayer (locus: paired with God hearing his pleas) - reactive devotion rather than moral disposition (#9) or law-love (#11).

narratives.narrative: Dabaq (sense 7680754), the cleaving verb, here as STATE (type 7680755) and pointed DOWNWARD: 'My soul clings to the dust; give me life according to your word!' The bearer (7680757) is the psalmist; the operation (7680758) is 'cling to the dust' - the clinging fastens not on God but on the dust, the low place of near-death. Strikingly the target (7680759) is 'none': the clinging to dust reaches toward no worthy object; it is a condition of being pressed low, not a movement of devotion. The coupling (7680761) is 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' - this clinging is one pole of a larger arc in Psalm 119 that runs from clinging to dust to clinging to God's testimonies. Locus internal:ib-state (7680762), role characteristic (7680764): the self clinging low, pleading revival (discovery 7680763). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the low state is not explained; NO seat (7680756='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7680760) - unqualified; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, no separately logged effect, no prohibition. The finding, held sharply distinct from 63:8: the SAME verb of total attachment can cleave downward to the dust of despair as readily as upward to God - here it registers the self flattened, glued to the ground, crying to be raised.
narratives.story: The same word for clinging that elsewhere means holding fast to God is turned downward here: 'My soul clings to the dust.' The psalmist is pressed so low he feels stuck to the ground, close to death, and his clinging reaches toward nothing good - it is simply the grip of despair. So he prays, 'Give me life according to your word.' The psalm does not explain how he sank so low or locate the ache in any one part of him. It shows a person flattened, glued to the dust, begging to be lifted. Clinging here is not devotion but the pull of the ground on a fainting soul.
narratives.variation_note: The DOWNWARD cling: same dabaq as 63:8 and 119:31, but its object is the DUST (target = none, locus internal), a state of despair rather than devotion - the low pole of the psalm's clinging arc.

narratives.narrative: Dabaq (sense 7680898) as action (type 7680899), now pointed toward the word: 'I cling to your testimonies, O LORD; let me not be put to shame!' The bearer (7680901) is the psalmist; the operation (7680902) is 'cling to the testimonies'; the target (7680903) is God's word. The coupling (7680905) is 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' - the upward answer to the downward clinging-to-dust of v25. Locus external:god (7680906), role characteristic (7680908): clinging fast to the word against the threat of shame (discovery 7680907). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the clinging is not derived; NO seat (7680900='none') - not organ-located, unlike 63:8 where the soul is named; manner 'none' (7680904) - unqualified; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, no separately logged effect, no prohibition. The finding, distinct from v25 and from 63:8: here the total-attachment verb fastens on God's TESTIMONIES rather than on God directly (63:8) or on the dust (v25) - devotion to the word as the thing held onto for dear life. Within Psalm 119's arc the movement is from clinging to dust to clinging to the word: the same grip, redirected from despair's ground to God's revelation.
narratives.story: Earlier in this long psalm the writer's soul clung to the dust in despair; now the same clinging is turned upward, but toward God's words: 'I hold fast to your instructions, LORD; do not let me be ashamed.' He grips the word the way a drowning man grips a rope. Here what he clings to is not God directly but everything God has said - the promises and commands he stakes his life on. The psalm does not explain how the clinging began or place it in any one part of him. The picture is a person who, having been flat in the dust, now fastens himself to God's word and refuses to be moved.
narratives.variation_note: Same dabaq, upward again but distinct from 63:8: the object is God's TESTIMONIES/word (external:god) rather than God himself, and no seat is named; within Ps 119 it is the answering pole to v25's clinging-to-dust.

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7681283) as disposition (type 7681284): 'I find my delight in your commandments, which I love.' The bearer (7681286) is the psalmist; the operation (7681287) is love; the target (7681288) is God's law / commandments / testimonies - the word itself. The coupling (7681290) is 'paired with the whole LOVE-arc of the psalm': this reading is the anchor for love of the word running right through Psalm 119, recurring at 119:48, 97, 113, 119, 127, 132, 159, 163, 165, 167. Locus external:god (7681291), role characteristic (7681293): love of the commandments is the very SPRING of the psalmist's delight (discovery 7681292). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the love is assumed as the settled disposition of the whole psalm; NO seat (7681285='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7681289) - unqualified; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, and the delight it produces is captured as the operation's spring rather than logged as a separate effect; no prohibition. The finding: love here has an unusual object - not God directly, nor his name, but his LAW. To love the commandments is to have one's delight sourced in them; across the psalm this love recurs so persistently that it functions as the settled temper of the devout interior, the affection that makes obedience a joy rather than a burden.
narratives.story: Running all through the longest psalm is one steady note: the writer loves God's commands. 'I delight in your commandments, because I love them.' His love is aimed at the word itself - not just at God, but at everything God has said - and that love is the source of his joy; keeping God's ways is a pleasure to him, not a chore. This same love for the word comes up again and again across the psalm. It is simply the settled temper of his heart. The psalm does not explain how it began or fix it in any one part of him; it shows a person whose deepest affection is bound to God's instruction.
narratives.variation_note: The anchor for love of the WORD across Psalm 119 (recurs at 10 further verses): target is God's law/commandments (external:god), the settled disposition whose fruit is delight - distinct from love of God's name (#2, #7), house (#3), salvation (#8) or God himself (#9, #10).

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7683509) as disposition (type 7683510): 'Your promise is well tried, and your servant loves it.' The bearer (7683512) is the psalmist; the operation (7683513) is love; the target (7683514) is God's law / commandments / testimonies - here specifically the PROMISE. The coupling (7683516) is 'paired with the whole LOVE-arc of the psalm'. Locus external:god (7683517), role characteristic (7683519): love of the tested, proven promise (discovery 7683518) - the servant loves the word precisely because it has been assayed and found pure. The silences: NO source (103 absent) as a formal row, though the verse itself supplies the ground (the promise is 'well tried'); NO seat (7683511='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7683515) - unqualified; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, no separately logged effect, no prohibition. The finding, distinct from the other 'loved' readings: this love is answered to WORTH tested by fire - the promise has proven itself, and the servant's love is the response of one who has handled the word and found it reliable. Where 45:7 loves righteousness and 109:17 loves cursing, here the loved object is the tried word of God, and the love has the character of settled trust in what has been proven true.
narratives.story: The psalmist looks at God's promise and says it has been tested and found completely pure - 'and your servant loves it.' His love here is aimed at the word, and specifically because it has proven itself reliable; it has been tried like metal in fire and come out true, and that is why he loves it. This is love as settled trust in something that has been proven. The psalm does not locate the love in any one part of him or measure it; it simply shows a servant who has handled God's promises, found them dependable, and loves them for it.
narratives.variation_note: The third 'loved' (aheb participle) reading: object is God's tested PROMISE/word (external:god), love as trust in what is proven - contrasting #1 (love of righteousness) and #2 (the enemy's love of cursing).

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7684649) as disposition (type 7684650): 'May they be secure who love you [Jerusalem]!' The bearer (7684652) is the pilgrims; the operation (7684653) is love; the target (7684654) is JERUSALEM - the holy city itself, a distinctive object among these readings. The coupling field (7684656) carries 'internal:ib-state', and the locus field (7684657) records the love as paired with 'praying for its peace': to love the city is bound up with interceding for it - 'Pray for the peace of Jerusalem.' Role characteristic (7684659): the lovers of the city are blessed with security (discovery 7684658). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the love is not derived; NO seat (7684651='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7684655) - unqualified; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, and the promised security is framed as a blessing sought rather than logged as the characteristic's own effect; no prohibition. The finding: love here reaches toward a place charged with God's presence (the city of the temple), and it expresses itself in prayer for that place's welfare. To love Jerusalem is not passive fondness but active intercession; the interior attachment issues in petition, and the lovers are themselves caught up in the peace they seek.
narratives.story: On pilgrimage to Jerusalem, the psalmist calls out, 'Pray for the peace of Jerusalem - may those who love you be secure.' The love here is aimed at the city itself, the place of God's temple, and it does not sit still: to love the city is to pray for its welfare. Loving and interceding go together. The psalm does not explain how this love arose or place it in any one part of the pilgrims; it simply shows that those who love the city long and pray for its good - and are themselves wrapped up in the peace they ask for. Love, here, prays.
narratives.variation_note: Unique target among aheb readings - JERUSALEM the city (place of God's presence), not God/his name/law - and its distinctive expression is intercession (locus: paired with praying for its peace).

narratives.narrative: Aheb (sense 7689481) as affect (type 7689482): 'The LORD preserves all who love him.' The bearer (7689484) is 'those who love'; the operation (7689485) is read as the love of God that HE PRESERVES - the interior attachment God guards. The target (7689486) is 'love-attachment', and the coupling (7689488, love-and-be-kept) welds the loving to being kept: to love God is to be preserved by him. Locus internal:ib-state (7689489), role characteristic (7689491): the self's fastening onto God in love, answered by preservation (discovery 7689490). The silences: NO source (103 absent) - the love is not derived; NO seat (7689483='none') - not organ-located; manner 'none' (7689487) - unqualified; intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109-113) - no measured degree, nothing further, and God's preserving is captured in the coupling rather than logged as a separate effect; no prohibition. The finding, closing the family: love here is the interior attachment that God himself keeps - the same movement that in 91:14 draws God's deliverance is here the mark of those God preserves, set in the psalm against the wicked whom he destroys. To love God is, in the end, to be held by him; the coupling love-and-be-kept states the whole relation in a phrase.
narratives.story: Near the close of a great psalm of praise comes a quiet assurance: 'The LORD watches over all who love him.' The love described is the heart's fastening onto God, and it is answered by his keeping - to love him is to be guarded by him. The two go together: loving and being kept are bound in a single phrase. This stands in sharp contrast to the wicked, whom the same verse says God will destroy. The psalm does not explain how the love began or place it in any one part of the person; it simply states the relation - those who love God are held safe by him. In the end, love means being kept.
narratives.variation_note: An affect reading (like #1-3) but positive and Godward: the love God PRESERVES, welded to being kept (coupling love-and-be-kept, internal locus); it closes the aheb arc that opened with disordered love of vanity (#1).
